source.title: Refusal Beyond a Single Direction: A Preliminary Comparison of Diff-in-Means and INLP

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies the difference-in-means direction and directional ablation/activation addition to new chat models, including an all-layer-and-position intervention in the appendix. It also compares those interventions with INLP.
record.gate_note: The study reports intervention outcomes for DiM and INLP. Selection scores and selected layer/token positions are used to choose settings, not recorded as results. Cited findings from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study applies the Arditi et al. difference-in-means direction, with directional ablation and activation addition, to five safety-tuned chat models. It uses Arditi's dataset construction and substring refusal metric, and includes the every-layer ablation recipe in Appendix E (Table 10). Its INLP results compare a different extraction method and do not measure a version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, with three additions. The authors say H1 is only partially supported. They state DiM remains the simpler primitive and the stronger baseline at its own selected layer. Their cross-site result concerns single-layer application, whereas all-layer application strengthens DiM ablation (e.g. Llama-2 +0.46 to +0.91).
record.recipe_differences: Uses the harmful-minus-harmless DiM contrast and directional ablation/activation addition, but compares these with INLP subspace projections and counterfactual flips. Main results intervene at a selected layer/token component; the appendix also reports every-layer-and-position results.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with INLP subspace size k, operator α, model, and selected application layer/token position. Cross-site results show the DiM ablation's effectiveness can be layer-dependent; counterfactual flipping is more robust in that check.

fits_no_version.finding: INLP nullspace projection leaves activations between the harmful and harmless clusters, while counterfactual flipping moves them into the opposite cluster. The authors read this tentatively as the model encoding concept absence differently from its opposite.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Erasing a refusal subspace gives an 'absence' state distinct from the harmless state; reflecting across it gives the opposite state.

fits_no_version.finding: INLP counterfactual flipping matches DiM ablation on refusal suppression in most models and is more layer-robust. INLP nullspace projection is weaker, failing on Llama-2. Subspace size k trades effect against perplexity, with mixed direction across models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alternative supervised linear extractors (INLP) can match DiM refusal steering, and DiM's apparent edge partly depends on its layer selection.

record.problems: The authors call the work preliminary and test only the smallest model from each of five families. Refusal metrics have documented substring/judge disagreement and bias; judge-based residual refusal results are mostly figures. Harmless-side induction under activation addition has coherence/perplexity costs. INLP layer selection used nullspace projection even when evaluating counterfactual flipping.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the all-layer unsafe-harmful metric, MMLU and ARC benchmark rows, selected-component DiM rows, all other INLP k-regimes, cross-site rows, ActAdd strength sweeps, judge diagnostics, and further appendix analyses. The paper reports these in Table 1 and Tables 3, 6–13 and Figures 7–17; the retained rows prioritize the direct all-layer V1 outcomes and the selected-component INLP comparisons relevant to V4.

untested.parts: No weight edit or released abliterated models.
No jailbreak attacks and no adversarial training against ablation.
No test of affine, cone, or dominant-plus-other structure. The INLP subspace-size comparisons are benchmarks of a different extraction method.
Harmfulness judgment versus the refusal decision is not separated.
No cross-language, cross-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer.
Only the smallest model in each of five families; no scale test.

missing.what: Selected-component (single-layer) DiM ablation non-refusal: Gemma +0.89, Qwen +0.67, Yi +0.60, Llama-2 +0.46, Llama-3 +0.95
Cross-site DiM ablation at INLP's layer: Qwen +0.03, Llama-2 +0.06, Llama-3 +0.20
MMLU/ARC deltas under all-layer ablation, all within about ±0.02
LlamaGuard 2 unsafe-harmful deltas under all-layer ablation (+0.56 to +0.82)
Judge-side residual refusals and partial request satisfaction under suppression
ActAdd strength sweep (x0.5, x2): x0.5 induces only +0.16 to +0.56 harmless refusal; x2 collapses perplexity

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. V1 rows r01–r05 are at or near substring ceilings: the ±0.00 SEs match the maximum values reached by other interventions. ActAdd is extraction-layer only in both scopes, so the record's 'every layer' condition is wrong for r06–r10 and r16–r20. INLP rows benchmark the study's comparison method and are relinked to none. The paper is a preprint calling itself preliminary; models are 1.8B–8B only.

versions.untested_parts: Tests DiM ablation and activation addition, harmful-prompt refusal suppression, harmless-prompt refusal induction, and capability measures. Does not test a weight edit, jailbreak mechanism, or transfer.
No conversion of ablation into a weight edit or released-model abliteration evaluation.
No jailbreak attack that suppresses the direction and no training against its ablation.
Compares INLP subspace interventions and their geometric effects with DiM; does not test affine or cone models explicitly, or establish a general dominant-direction-plus-others account.
Reports safety/unsafety metrics alongside refusal but does not test whether harmfulness judgment is separately represented from the refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or other transfer test.
No varied refusal-training method, timing, or stage; tested models are safety-fine-tuned chat models.

labels.reason: Induction +0.86 to +1.00, but Pile PPL falls (Gemma -1.00, others -0.10 to -0.27). The paper calls the induction partly a looping artefact, and the judge finds ActAdd destroys harmless utility (§5.3, D.2).

labels.reason: §D.2 (Figs 7, 10): no intervention takes the judge refusal share to zero, and suppression widens hedged compliance. Caveat: the authors find the judge over-fires by about 15 pp.

relation.reason: Reports its own ablation and addition results on five chat models, with capability measures.

tranche.reason: Uses Arditi's DiM direction, datasets and substring metric. Table 10 reproduces all-layer directional ablation, and ActAdd is at the extraction layer as in Arditi. The INLP comparison is an addition.

source_check.notes: Table 10 is garbled in the text. Qwen's Pile column was placed by cell adjacency, and Tables 6 and 10 give the same ActAdd values, so ActAdd is never all-layer. Only deltas are reported, not raw baseline rates. Whether the ActAdd PPL comes from adding or subtracting is not stated. Gemma '2B-IT' cites the Gemma 2 report, so the exact checkpoint is unclear.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: All five models, DiM ablation at every layer and position; harmless prompts under DiM activation addition
reader_labels.reason: All-layer DiM ablation yields large non-refusal increases (r01–r05), and activation addition strongly raises harmless-prompt refusal (r06–r10).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: All-layer suppression and activation addition, across the tested models
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that residual refusals remain, and all-layer activation addition worsens Pile perplexity in every model (r16–r20); therefore broad capability preservation is not established for addition.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: INLP subspace and α-operator comparisons at the selected component
reader_labels.reason: INLP methods yield different refusal-suppression strengths across models and k values (r21–r40), and the two operators produce qualitatively distinct activation geometries (r41–r42).
